To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the haptically guided exploration of tools, but not the subsequent grasp planning and grasp execution, engages left-lateralized temporo-parietofrontal networks.

haptic interactions with tools, as compared to non-tools, are associated with significant increases of left-lateralized temporo-parietofrontal activity and that the subsequent execution of functionally appropriate tool grasps is associated with significant increases only of dorsal cortical activity.

haptically driven functional grasping of objects activates the temporo-paraito-frontal network in the left hemisphere, but only in the later stage of processing, when the functional grasp is executed, not when the object is explored.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the haptically guided grasp of tools is mediated at the neuronal and functional level by a network of cortical regions that are only partly overlapping with those engaged in the visual guidance of actions with tools.

the temporo-pariot-frontal networks responsive for interactions with tools are recruited during the early stages of haptically directed tool use, but are not necessary for the later execution phase of functional grasping, at least in a context where the grasp has been pre-planned.
the haptic processing of tools is not fully lateralized, but rather is characterized by a more complex and distributed pattern of cortical activations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the neural basis of tool use is not as unitary as it is often assumed, and that the haptic and visual systems are not functionally equivalent.

the neural basis of haptically-guided tool-directed actions is more complex than previously assumed, and that the exploration phase of tool-directed grasping is not only about extracting the structural properties of the tool, but also about the planning of functionally adequate grasping.
haptically directed tool use is a complex cognitive task, and that the neural mechanisms supporting this task are not fully understood yet.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the haptic exploration of a tool is a crucial step in the planning and subsequent execution of a functional grasp.
, although the neural bases of tool-directed actions are largely shared across sensory modalities, they are also modality-specific.
the haptic modality, like the visual modality, is associated with a left-lateralized cortical network that supports the planning and execution of functional grasps of tools.
